title: Airbnb vs. host: Who is responsible for collecting and remitting STR taxes?
summary: Don't assume Airbnb handles your short-term rental taxes. Learn where platform responsibility ends, your local liabilities begin, and how to stay compliant.

# Airbnb vs. host: Who is responsible for collecting and remitting STR taxes?


by


[Guesty Marketing Team](https://www.guesty.com/blog/author/guesty-marketing-team/)


|


August 26, 2026 Reading time: 7 minutes


Share


Share


If you assume Airbnb handles all your local tax compliance automatically, check your local laws right now. The platform collects and remits taxes in many jurisdictions, but it misses plenty of them. Get this wrong, and you face severe penalties, back taxes, and a suspended operating license.


Tax collection shifts depending on where your property sits and which platforms process your reservations, leaving you with the ultimate responsibility for compliance. Learn exactly where the platform’s responsibility ends and yours begins.


**TL;DR**


- Airbnb automatically collects and remits occupancy taxes only in jurisdictions with active platform agreements.
- You must manually collect and remit taxes in cities or counties without an Airbnb collection agreement.
- Direct bookings and alternative channels shift the tax burden entirely back to you as the merchant of record.
- Cleaning fees, pet fees, and extra guest charges often count as taxable gross revenue.
- Filing a return remains mandatory in many cities, even if the platform handles 100 percent of the remittance.
- A vacation rental software like Guesty® tracks revenue across every channel, so you pull exactly what you need for quarterly tax filings without manual math.


## How location and booking channels determine tax responsibility


Short-term rental taxes go by many names, including occupancy, lodging, or hotel taxes. These requirements are highly localized, meaning a single reservation often triggers state, county, and city taxes simultaneously.


Every local government dictates how short-term rentals operate within its borders. Some cities force booking platforms to collect taxes at the point of sale, while others demand that the property manager handle the funds directly.


Distributing listings across multiple platforms introduces fragmented tax policies. Airbnb might collect and remit your county taxes automatically, whereas Booking.com might require you to collect them yourself. Vrbo and Expedia follow entirely different timelines based on their specific legal agreements with your city. ## Airbnb occupancy tax collection models


Airbnb handles local taxes through two distinct mechanisms, applying the correct model based entirely on local legislation.


First is the automatic collection and remittance model. Airbnb charges the guest the local tax rate at checkout and holds these funds. At the end of the reporting period, Airbnb pays the local tax authority directly. You never touch this money, as the transaction happens entirely behind the scenes.


Second is the pass-through tax model. Airbnb still charges the guest the tax at checkout, but instead of paying the government, the platform sends the tax funds directly to your payout account alongside your nightly rate. You must hold these funds and remit them to the local tax authority on schedule.


When a guest books a five-night stay in a pass-through tax jurisdiction, the booking platform deposits the nightly rate, cleaning fee, and tax lump sum into your main operating account. This tax revenue mixes with general funds before the quarterly remittance deadline arrives.


### Check your Airbnb tax collection status


Never guess your compliance status. Verify exactly what the platform handles for your specific listing by opening your hosting dashboard. Navigate to your account settings and select the taxes section to review the occupancy tax details for every individual property.


The dashboard displays whether Airbnb collects and remits taxes for your jurisdiction automatically. If you see an option to add custom taxes, you operate in an area where the burden falls on you.


## When the tax burden falls entirely on you


Airbnb negotiates collection agreements jurisdiction by jurisdiction, leaving thousands of cities, counties, and municipalities without any platform agreement in place. If your property sits in one of these locations, you carry 100 percent of the tax burden.


You must calculate the local tax rate and either add it to your listing price or configure it as a separate line item. You then collect the funds, hold them safely, and file the returns with your local government.

This burden also shifts when you expand beyond Airbnb, as other online travel agencies operate under different rules. A city might have an active agreement with Airbnb but lack one with Booking.com, forcing you to collect and remit the taxes for those specific reservations yourself.


### Tax management for direct bookings


Launching your own site to avoid OTA commissions makes you the merchant of record. Build a branded site that captures reservations directly. Guesty® is a[vacation rental software](https://www.guesty.com/) that powers your direct booking engine, letting you set your exact tax rates once so they apply automatically at checkout.


When a guest books directly, no platform acts as a middleman. You process the payment, collect the tax, and file the return. Your direct booking revenue requires the strictest financial tracking because the local government views you as the sole responsible entity.


## The zero-dollar tax return trap


Failing to file a return when you owe nothing is the most common compliance error in short-term rental management.


Many operators see that Airbnb collects and remits their local taxes perfectly, assuming their tax obligation is finished. They stop filing quarterly returns, causing the city to flag their account for delinquency, issue a fine, and threaten their operating license.


Even when platforms remit 100 percent of the tax owed, the city requires you to prove it. Because you hold the local business license, you must file a monthly or quarterly return reporting your total gross receipts for the period. You then claim a deduction for the exact amount of revenue processed by platforms with active collection agreements.


The resulting math leaves you with a zero-dollar balance owed. Submitting this zero-dollar return maintains your compliance.


City revenue departments audit active short-term rental licenses regularly. When an active license shows zero reporting history, algorithms flag the account for non-compliance, triggering a manual audit even if the platform paid every cent it owed.


## What exactly counts as taxable revenue?


Guests pay multiple fees on top of the nightly rate, and local tax authorities want their cut of the entire transaction.


Occupancy taxes generally apply to the gross amount paid by the guest, including the nightly rate, cleaning fees, extra guest fees, and pet fees. If the guest pays a mandatory charge to stay at your property, the local government usually considers it taxable revenue.


Refundable security deposits do not count as taxable revenue. If you collect a deposit and return it to the guest after checkout, that money escapes the occupancy tax. If the guest damages the property and you keep the deposit, that retained amount may become taxable depending on local rules.

## Centralize your financial reporting across channels


Fragmented tax data creates massive operational risks. You cannot afford to guess which reservations included tax collection and which ones passed the burden to you.

You waste hours manually extracting cleaning fees, nightly rates, and tax line items just to figure out your gross receipts for the quarter. One calculation error results in underpaying your local government or double-paying taxes the platform already remitted.


Pulling tax data from four different booking platforms turns quarterly filing into a manual extraction project.
